question:
Patient note:
A 63-year-old man with an eight-year history of genetically confirmed hereditary hemochromatosis complicated by portal hypertension and nodular cirrhosis arrived at the tertiary-care hepatology walk-in suite after noticing gradually progressive abdominal fullness, a snugger waistband, and dark tea-colored urine over the preceding three weeks. He reported mild fatigue that curtailed his usual routine of cycling four miles each morning, yet he continued to attend his job as a high-school physics teacher without difficulty and denied any episodes of confusion, daytime somnolence, disorientation, personality change, flapping tremor, falls, or difficulties balancing the school’s budget spreadsheet. He had remained abstinent from alcohol since his diagnosis and had never used illicit drugs; he stopped smoking pipes twenty years earlier. Prior medical conditions included well-controlled type 2 diabetes managed with sitagliptin 100 mg daily, stage 1 chronic kidney disease with a baseline creatinine around 1.1 mg/dL, and remote peptic ulcer disease for which he took no current acid-suppressive therapy. Phlebotomies had been performed monthly during the first three years after diagnosis, and serum ferritin had been stable below 200 ng/mL for the last two years; he was not taking any chelating agents. He used no herbal supplements, had no known drug allergies, and was fully vaccinated against hepatitis A and B. Family history was notable for a brother who died suddenly from myocardial infarction at age 60; there was no familial liver disease other than his own. Review of systems was negative for hematemesis, melena, hematochezia, pruritus, fevers, chills, night sweats, unintentional weight change, shortness of breath when lying flat, ankle swelling that limited footwear, or recent antibiotic exposure. On arrival he was seated upright and conversant, vital signs showing temperature 36.9 °C, blood pressure 122/78 mm Hg, heart rate 84 beats/min, respiratory rate 14 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 98 % while breathing ambient air. He answered orientation questions rapidly, spelled “world” backward without hesitation, and completed serial threes to twenty in under fifteen seconds. Sclerae were faintly icteric, conjunctivae were moist and pink, and there were a handful of spider angiomata scattered over the shoulders. Oral mucosa was moist without a sweet or musty odor. Cardiovascular examination revealed a normal S1 and S2 without murmurs or extra sounds; lung fields were clear to percussion and auscultation. Abdominal inspection disclosed a rounded contour with slight bulging of the flanks, yet the umbilicus remained inverted. Light percussion demonstrated tympany across the anterior abdomen, transitioning to dullness laterally; when the patient rolled toward the left side, the zone of dullness migrated toward the dependent flank, and an assistant-supported fluid-wave maneuver transmitted a small impulse across the midline. Palpation identified a firm, mildly nodular liver edge palpable 3 cm below the right costal margin on deep inspiration; the spleen tip was not felt. The abdominal wall was soft and non-tender, and there were no abdominal collaterals. Lower extremities revealed trace pitting edema over the ankles; there was no calf tenderness. Neurologic screening showed intact cranial nerves, symmetrical strength, brisk deep tendon reflexes, normal rapid alternating movements, and absence of asterixis when the arms were extended for 30 seconds. A point-of-care ultrasound performed before venipuncture confirmed a coarse, echogenic liver surface with serrated contour, patent portal and hepatic veins exhibiting hepatopetal flow at 14 cm/s, and an anechoic stripe of fluid measuring approximately 2.5 cm in maximal depth along the right paracolic gutter; no focal hepatic masses or portal vein thrombosis were evident. Laboratory studies obtained immediately afterward, before any diuretic or albumin administration, revealed: total bilirubin 3.2 mg/dL, serum albumin 2.9 g/dL, alanine aminotransferase 58 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 80 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 162 U/L, gamma-glutamyl transferase 175 U/L, sodium 136 mmol/L, potassium 4.3 mmol/L, chloride 100 mmol/L, bicarbonate 24 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 20 mg/dL, creatinine 1.1 mg/dL, fasting glucose 142 mg/dL, hemoglobin 12.4 g/dL, platelet count 110 × 10⁹/L, white blood cell count 6.1 × 10⁹/L, and a prothrombin time corresponding to an international normalized ratio of 2.15. Serum ferritin was 180 ng/mL and transferrin saturation 43 %. Hepatitis C antibody remained negative, and alpha-fetoprotein measured 7 ng/mL. Urinalysis demonstrated moderate bilirubin, 1+ urobilinogen, no proteinuria, and no evidence of infection. A portable upright chest radiograph showed elevated hemidiaphragms without pleural effusions, and a 12-lead electrocardiogram recorded normal sinus rhythm at 80 beats/min with no acute ischemic changes. Given the evolving abdominal fluid accumulation, mild jaundice, modest synthetic dysfunction reflected by the reduced albumin concentration and prolonged coagulation parameters, and the absence of cognitive impairment or gross motor disturbance, the clinical impression was a recent decompensation of iron-overload cirrhosis manifesting primarily with new peritoneal fluid and worsening jaundice in the context of preserved mentation.

Question: What is the patient's Child-Pugh Score? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Child-Pugh score assigns 1–3 points each for bilirubin, albumin, INR, ascites, and hepatic encephalopathy. Using pretreatment findings:
- Total bilirubin 3.2 mg/dL (>3): 3 points.
- Albumin 2.9 g/dL (2.8–3.5): 2 points.
- INR 2.15 (1.7–2.3): 2 points.
- Ascites (none/slight/moderate-to-severe = 1/2/3): abdominal enlargement with bulging flanks, shifting dullness, and a fluid wave supports clinically moderate ascites: 3 points.
- Encephalopathy (none/grade I–II/grade III–IV = 1/2/3): normal orientation and attention without asterixis: 1 point.
Total = 3 + 2 + 2 + 3 + 1 = 11.
Final answer: 11
